passages.q: Why do so many prices end in 99?
p: A price of £4.99 is only one penny less than £5.00, yet shops use such prices everywhere. If customers were perfectly logical, the penny would make no difference. Research suggests it does, because of the way people read numbers.

We read prices from left to right and give the first digit the most weight. So £4.99 is often filed in the mind as “four pounds something” rather than “nearly five”. Psychologists call this the left-digit effect. It is strongest when people glance quickly, which is how most shopping happens.

Prices ending in 99 also signal something. Shoppers have learned to associate them with discounts and value, while round numbers such as £50 can suggest quality and confidence. That is why luxury brands often avoid .99 endings. The choice of the last digits is not just about the penny; it tells customers what kind of product they are looking at.
g: Prices end in .99 because, although logically the penny is trivial, research shows it changes how people judge prices.
The left-digit effect explains it, because people weigh the first digit most when they glance at prices.
Endings also send signals, because .99 suggests value while round prices suggest quality, so luxury brands avoid .99.
k: A one-penny difference should not matter logically, but it does.
People weigh the first digit most: the left-digit effect.
.99 signals value; round numbers signal quality, so luxury brands avoid .99.

mc.s: What is the passage mainly about?
o: Why price endings influence how customers judge prices
Why customers are illogical about everything
mc.e: It explains the left-digit effect and the signalling role of price endings.

mc.s: A high-end watch brand prices a watch at £3,000 rather than £2,999. Why, according to the passage?
o: A round price suggests quality and confidence
The left-digit effect does not exist
mc.e: The third paragraph says round numbers can signal quality, which is why luxury brands avoid .99.

mc.s: When is the left-digit effect strongest?
o: When people glance at prices quickly
mc.e: The second paragraph says it is strongest when people glance quickly.

v.d: To associate one thing with another is to link them in your mind.
To signal something is to suggest or communicate it, often without saying it directly.

passages.q: How do plants turn sunlight into the material they are made of?
p: A large tree can weigh many tonnes, yet very little of that mass comes from the soil. Most of it comes from the air. Plants build their bodies largely from carbon dioxide, using a process called photosynthesis.

Inside leaf cells are tiny structures called chloroplasts, which contain the green pigment chlorophyll. Chlorophyll absorbs light energy, mostly red and blue light, and reflects green, which is why leaves look green. The plant uses this energy to split water drawn up from its roots, and to combine carbon dioxide from the air into sugars. Oxygen is released as a by-product.

Those sugars are the plant’s fuel and its building material. Some are burned for energy; others are turned into cellulose, the tough fibre that makes up wood and stems. Almost all life on Earth depends on photosynthesis, either directly by eating plants or indirectly by eating animals that did. Even the oxygen we breathe comes mostly from it.
g: Most of a plant’s mass comes from the air, because plants build themselves from carbon dioxide by photosynthesis.
Chlorophyll captures light, so the plant can split water and turn carbon dioxide into sugars, releasing oxygen.
The sugars fuel and build the plant, and almost all life depends on photosynthesis for food and oxygen.
k: Plants build most of their mass from carbon dioxide in the air.
Chlorophyll absorbs light; the energy turns water and carbon dioxide into sugars and releases oxygen.
Sugars fuel and build plants; nearly all life depends on photosynthesis.

mc.s: What does the passage explain?
o: How plants use light to build themselves from carbon dioxide
Why soil is important for trees
mc.e: It goes from where plant mass comes from, to how photosynthesis works, to why it matters.

mc.s: What would most surprise someone who thinks trees are made from soil?
o: Most of a tree’s mass comes from the air
mc.e: The first paragraph directly contradicts the soil idea.

mc.s: Why do leaves look green?
mc.e: The second paragraph says chlorophyll absorbs red and blue and reflects green.

v.d: A pigment is a substance that gives something its colour.

o: something produced as a side effect of another process
v.d: A by-product is an extra result produced while making something else.

passages.q: What was the Silk Road, and what travelled along it besides silk?
p: The Silk Road was not a single road. It was a shifting network of overland and sea routes linking China, Central Asia, India, Persia, Arabia and the Mediterranean, used for well over a thousand years. The name itself came much later, coined by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen in 1877.

Few traders travelled the whole distance. Goods moved in stages, passing from merchant to merchant and city to city, with prices rising at every step. Silk, spices, tea, horses, glass, paper and precious metals all changed hands, and great trading cities such as Samarkand grew rich on the traffic.

The most important cargo was often invisible. Religions such as Buddhism and later Islam spread along the routes. So did technologies like papermaking, mathematical ideas and new crops. Diseases travelled too: the plague that devastated Europe in the fourteenth century is thought to have spread partly along these trade networks. Connection brought wealth and ideas, and also risk.
g: The Silk Road was a long-lasting network of land and sea routes, named only in the nineteenth century.
Goods passed in stages through many traders, so prices rose along the way and trading cities prospered.
Ideas, religions, technologies and diseases also travelled, so connection brought both benefits and risks.
k: The Silk Road was a network of routes, not one road, named in 1877.
Goods moved in stages through many merchants; trading cities like Samarkand grew rich.
Religions, technologies and diseases also spread along it.

mc.s: What is the main idea?
o: The Silk Road was a network that moved goods, ideas and diseases across continents
The Silk Road was a single road built by China
Silk was the only valuable good traded
Traders usually travelled the whole route
mc.e: The passage corrects the single-road idea and stresses what else travelled.

mc.s: Why did prices rise along the route?
o: Each merchant in the chain added their own cost and profit
mc.e: The second paragraph says goods passed through many hands, with prices rising at each step.

mc.s: What does the phrase “the most important cargo was often invisible” introduce?
o: Ideas, beliefs and diseases rather than physical goods
Goods that were lost on the way
Silk that was too fine to see
mc.e: The third paragraph lists religions, technologies and diseases.

o: invented a new word or phrase
v.d: To coin a term is to invent it.
To devastate is to destroy or badly damage.

passages.q: What is Moore’s law, and is it really a law?
p: In 1965 Gordon Moore, who later co-founded Intel, noticed that the number of components that could be fitted onto a computer chip was doubling at a steady rate. In 1975 he revised his estimate to a doubling roughly every two years. The prediction became known as Moore’s law.

For decades it held remarkably well. Transistors shrank, chips became faster and cheaper, and computing power that once filled a room fitted into a pocket. The steady pace also became a target: chip makers planned their research to keep up with it, so the prediction helped make itself come true.

But Moore’s law is an observation about engineering and economics, not a law of physics. As transistors approach the size of a few atoms, shrinking them further becomes harder and far more expensive, and the pace has slowed. Progress now comes increasingly from new chip designs, specialised processors and better software, rather than simply from making everything smaller.
g: Moore observed in 1965 that chip components doubled regularly, later estimated as every two years.
The prediction held for decades and also became a target, so it partly made itself come true.
It is not a physical law, so as transistors near atomic size progress slows and comes from new designs instead.
k: Moore observed chip components doubling roughly every two years.
It held for decades and became a self-fulfilling industry target.
It is not a law of physics; shrinking is slowing, and gains now come from new designs and software.

mc.s: What is the passage’s main point?
o: Moore’s law was a powerful observation and target, but not a physical law, and it is slowing
mc.e: The passage describes the law, its success, and its limits.

mc.s: In what sense did Moore’s law help make itself come true?
o: Companies planned research to hit its pace
It changed the laws of physics
mc.e: The second paragraph says it became a target that chip makers planned around.

mc.s: Where does progress increasingly come from now?
o: New chip designs, specialised processors and better software
mc.e: The final sentence lists these.

v.d: To revise an estimate is to change it after looking at it again.
Specialised processors are built to do particular kinds of task very efficiently.

passages.q: Why do people tend to find evidence for what they already believe?
p: People do not simply weigh evidence and reach conclusions. They tend to look for, notice and remember information that supports what they already think, and to discount information that does not. Psychologists call this confirmation bias.

In a classic experiment by Peter Wason in 1960, people were given the sequence 2, 4, 6 and asked to discover the rule behind it by testing other sequences. Most tested sequences like 8, 10, 12 that fitted their guess, such as “even numbers going up by two”. Few tried sequences that might prove their guess wrong. The actual rule was simply “any increasing numbers”.

The lesson is that testing ideas well means seeking evidence that could disprove them. In business, this might mean asking what would have to be true for a strategy to fail, or deliberately seeking out the customers who left. Feeling confident is not the same as having tested a belief against its strongest challenge.
g: People favour information that supports their existing beliefs, a tendency called confirmation bias.
Wason’s 2-4-6 task shows this, because people tested only sequences that fitted their guess and missed the real rule.
Good thinking seeks evidence that could disprove an idea, so in business ask how a plan could fail.
k: Confirmation bias: favouring information that supports what we already believe.
In Wason’s 2-4-6 task, people tested confirming cases and missed the simple rule.
Test ideas by seeking evidence that could prove them wrong.

mc.s: What is the passage mainly about?
o: Confirmation bias and how to counter it
mc.e: It defines the bias, gives an experiment, then gives advice.

mc.s: Which test would have helped people in Wason’s task most?
o: Trying 1, 2, 3, which breaks their guessed rule
mc.e: Testing sequences that do not fit your guess is how you discover it is wrong.

mc.s: A team is sure a new product will succeed. What would the passage suggest?
o: Ask what would have to be true for it to fail
mc.e: The third paragraph recommends seeking evidence that could disprove a belief.

v.d: To discount information is to give it less weight or ignore it.
To disprove something is to show it is not true.

passages.q: Why do concert tickets sometimes resell for many times their face value?
p: A popular band sells tickets for £70, and they are gone within minutes. Soon the same tickets appear on resale sites for £400. Who is setting that price, and why does the gap exist?

Prices in a market tend to settle where the number of people wanting to buy matches the number of items available. A venue has a fixed number of seats, so supply cannot rise. If far more fans want to go than there are seats, the price at which demand matches supply is much higher than £70. Resellers capture the difference.

So why do bands not simply charge more? Many deliberately keep prices below the market level, believing it is fairer to fans and better for their reputation. Some use queues, ballots or ID checks to keep tickets with real fans. Each approach has trade-offs. Low prices that are allocated by speed can reward those with the fastest internet or the most bots, rather than the biggest fans.
g: Tickets sold for £70 can resell for £400, which raises the question of who sets the price and why.
Prices rise to where demand meets supply, and with fixed seats and many fans that price is far above face value.
Bands keep prices low for fairness and reputation, but every allocation method has trade-offs.
k: Popular tickets can resell for several times face value.
With fixed supply and high demand, the market price is far above face value; resellers capture the gap.
Artists keep prices low for fairness, but every allocation method has trade-offs.

mc.s: What does the passage explain?
o: Why a gap exists between face value and resale price, and how artists respond
mc.e: It explains the gap through supply and demand and then discusses artists’ choices.

mc.s: If a venue added many more seats for the same concert, what would likely happen to resale prices?
mc.e: More supply would bring the market price closer to face value.

mc.s: What does the last paragraph add?
o: Why artists choose below-market prices and the trade-offs involved
mc.e: It asks why bands do not raise prices and discusses their alternatives.

v.d: To capture value or a difference is to take it as profit.
To allocate is to decide who gets what.

passages.q: How does the heart keep blood moving around the body?
p: The human heart beats around 100,000 times a day without rest. It is a muscular pump about the size of a fist, divided into four chambers: two upper atria, which receive blood, and two lower ventricles, which push it out.

The heart actually runs two circuits at once. The right side receives blood that has delivered its oxygen to the body and pumps it to the lungs, where it picks up fresh oxygen. The left side receives this oxygen-rich blood from the lungs and pumps it out to the rest of the body. The left ventricle has the thickest wall, because it has to push blood the farthest.

Valves between the chambers act like one-way doors, so blood cannot flow backwards. The sound of a heartbeat is largely the noise of these valves closing. The rhythm is set by a small cluster of cells that produce electrical pulses, the heart’s natural pacemaker, which is why the heart can keep beating even without signals from the brain.
g: The heart is a four-chambered muscular pump that beats about 100,000 times a day.
It runs two circuits, so the right side sends blood to the lungs and the left side sends oxygen-rich blood to the body.
Valves keep blood flowing one way, and a natural pacemaker sets the rhythm, so the heart beats on its own.
k: The heart has four chambers: two atria receive, two ventricles pump.
The right side pumps to the lungs; the left side, with the thickest wall, pumps to the body.
One-way valves make the heartbeat sound; a natural pacemaker sets the rhythm.

mc.s: What is the passage about?
o: How the heart’s structure keeps blood moving in two circuits
How to keep the heart healthy
mc.e: It covers chambers, circuits, valves and rhythm.

mc.s: Why is the left ventricle’s wall thickest?
o: It must pump blood all around the body
It pumps only to the lungs
mc.e: The second paragraph says it has to push blood the farthest.

mc.s: What is the heartbeat sound mainly made by?
mc.e: The third paragraph says the sound is largely valves closing.

v.d: Here chambers are the hollow compartments inside the heart.
A cluster is a group of similar things close together.

passages.q: How does the Panama Canal get ships across mountains?
p: Before the Panama Canal opened in 1914, a ship sailing from New York to San Francisco had to go all the way around South America. The canal cut thousands of miles from the journey by crossing the narrow land of Panama. But Panama is not flat, and a sea-level canal proved impractical.

Instead, engineers built locks: giant water-filled chambers with gates at each end. A ship enters a lock, the gates close, and water flows in from above, raising the ship like a toy in a bath. Through a series of locks, ships climb about 26 metres to Gatun Lake, an artificial lake created by damming a river. They cross the lake, then descend through more locks to the other ocean.

Remarkably, the system uses no pumps to move this water. Gravity does the work, letting water flow down from the lake into the locks. The cost is that every ship passage releases a vast amount of fresh water to the sea, which is why droughts in Panama can force limits on how many ships cross.
g: The canal saved ships a long trip around South America, but Panama’s hills made a sea-level canal impractical.
Locks raise ships in steps to an artificial lake, so they can cross and then descend to the other ocean.
Gravity powers the locks, so each passage uses lots of fresh water and droughts can limit crossings.
k: The 1914 canal saved a long journey but had to cross hilly land.
Locks raise ships about 26 metres to Gatun Lake and lower them on the other side.
Gravity moves the water, so each crossing uses much fresh water; droughts limit traffic.

mc.s: What does the passage explain?
o: How locks lift ships across Panama and the water cost involved
The history of New York’s harbour
mc.e: It covers the problem, the lock solution and the water limitation.

mc.s: Why would a drought limit the number of ships crossing?
o: Each crossing releases lake water that is not replaced quickly
Ships cannot sail in hot weather
mc.e: The last paragraph links each passage to fresh water loss.

mc.s: How high do ships climb to reach Gatun Lake?
mc.e: The second paragraph says about 26 metres.

o: not sensible or workable in reality
v.d: Impractical means unrealistic or too difficult to do in practice.
To descend is to move downwards.

passages.t: The myth of the first mover
passages.q: Is being first to a market really an advantage?
p: It is often assumed that the first company into a new market wins. Being first can bring real benefits: a head start in building a brand, locking in customers and learning the market before rivals. Business writers call this first-mover advantage.

Yet history is full of pioneers that lost. Early search engines, social networks and smartphones were overtaken by later entrants. Studies of many industries have found that market pioneers often fail or lose leadership, while “fast followers” who enter a little later do well. Followers can learn from the pioneer’s mistakes, use better technology and enter once customers understand what they want.

The real question is not whether to be first, but whether being first creates something hard to copy. Where there are strong network effects, scarce resources or high switching costs, an early lead can last. Where the product is easy to imitate and the market is still unclear, being first may simply mean paying to educate customers for someone else.
g: Many assume the first company in a market wins, because being first offers a head start.
But pioneers often lose, because later entrants learn from their mistakes and enter once the market is clear.
So the key is whether being first creates something hard to copy; otherwise it may just help rivals.
k: First movers can gain brand, customers and learning.
Many pioneers lose to fast followers who learn from mistakes and enter when demand is clear.
Being first matters only if it creates a hard-to-copy advantage.

mc.s: What is the author’s main claim?
o: Being first helps only when it creates an advantage others cannot easily copy
mc.e: The final paragraph reframes the question around hard-to-copy advantages.

mc.s: In which market would being first matter most?
o: One where products are easy to copy
One where customers are unsure what they want
mc.e: The passage lists network effects, scarce resources and switching costs as conditions for a lasting lead.

mc.s: How does the second paragraph relate to the first?
o: It challenges the assumption described in the first
It gives more benefits of being first
mc.e: It begins with “Yet” and gives evidence against the common assumption.

v.d: Pioneers are the first people or companies to enter a new area.
To imitate is to copy something.

passages.q: Why do we yawn, and why is it contagious?
p: Almost all animals with backbones yawn, from fish to humans, and unborn babies yawn in the womb. Yet scientists still disagree about why. Yawning is a good example of a familiar behaviour that remains poorly understood.

An old idea is that yawning brings in more oxygen when we are tired. Experiments have not supported this: breathing extra oxygen does not reduce yawning. A newer idea is that yawning helps cool the brain, since a deep intake of air and the stretch of the jaw increase blood flow. Some studies find people yawn more when the air is cooler than their body, but the theory is still debated.

The contagious part is equally intriguing. Seeing, hearing or even reading about yawning makes many people yawn. Some research links this to social bonding, finding it more common between friends and family than between strangers, though results have been mixed. For now, the honest answer is that we have several plausible theories and no settled explanation.
g: Nearly all vertebrates yawn, but scientists still disagree about why.
The oxygen idea has not held up, and the brain-cooling idea has some support but is still debated.
Contagious yawning may relate to social bonding, but findings are mixed, so there is no settled answer.
k: Yawning is near-universal in vertebrates but poorly understood.
The oxygen theory lacks support; the brain-cooling theory is plausible but debated.
Contagious yawning may relate to social bonds; evidence is mixed and no explanation is settled.

mc.s: What is the author’s overall conclusion?
o: There are plausible theories about yawning but no settled explanation
Yawning is caused by lack of oxygen
Yawning cools the brain, proven beyond doubt
mc.e: The final sentence states this directly.

mc.s: Why do experiments with extra oxygen matter?
o: If oxygen caused yawning, extra oxygen should reduce it, but it does not
They prove yawning cools the brain
They show fish do not yawn
mc.e: The experiment tests a prediction of the oxygen theory, which failed.

mc.s: Why does the author describe yawning as “a good example”?
o: To show that even familiar behaviours can be poorly understood
To prove that science is useless
mc.e: The first paragraph frames yawning as an example of the limits of current knowledge.

o: spreading from one person to another
v.d: Contagious means able to spread from one person to another, here by seeing or hearing it.
A plausible idea seems believable but has not been proven.

passages.q: What does GDP measure, and what does it leave out?
p: Gross domestic product, or GDP, is the total value of goods and services produced in a country over a period, usually a year or a quarter. It is the most widely used measure of an economy’s size, and changes in it are how recessions and booms are identified.

But GDP measures market activity, not well-being. Unpaid work, such as caring for children or elderly relatives, does not appear in it, even though it is enormously valuable. Pollution can even raise GDP, if money is spent cleaning it up. And GDP says nothing about how income is shared: an economy can grow while most people’s incomes stay flat.

Simon Kuznets, who helped develop national income accounting in the 1930s, warned that such figures should not be read as a measure of a nation’s welfare. Many governments now supplement it with measures of well-being, inequality and environmental health. GDP remains useful, but it answers a narrower question than it is often asked to.
g: GDP is the total value of goods and services a country produces, used to measure economic size and cycles.
It measures market activity, not well-being, so unpaid work, pollution and inequality are missed or distorted.
Even its developer warned against treating it as welfare, so governments now add other measures.
k: GDP is the total value of goods and services produced, used to track booms and recessions.
It misses unpaid work, can rise with pollution costs, and ignores how income is shared.
Kuznets warned it is not a welfare measure; other indicators now supplement it.

mc.s: What is the passage’s main argument?
o: GDP is useful but measures less than people often assume
mc.e: It describes GDP’s use, its blind spots, and concludes it answers a narrower question.

mc.s: A parent leaves a paid job to care for their child full time. What happens to GDP?
o: It falls, even though valuable work is still being done
mc.e: Paid work counts in GDP but unpaid care does not.

mc.s: Who warned against reading national income as a measure of welfare?
mc.e: The third paragraph names Simon Kuznets.

v.d: Welfare here means people’s overall well-being, not only state benefits.

o: add to something to make it more complete
v.d: In the passage, the idea is that other measures are added alongside GDP; to supplement is to add to something.

passages.q: How did scientists come to accept that continents move?
p: Look at a map and the coasts of South America and Africa seem to fit together like puzzle pieces. In 1912 the German scientist Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents had once been joined and had slowly drifted apart. He pointed to matching fossils and rock formations on opposite sides of oceans.
Most geologists rejected the idea for decades. Wegener could not explain what force could push entire continents through the solid ocean floor, and without a mechanism the theory seemed far-fetched.

The breakthrough came in the 1950s and 1960s, when mapping of the ocean floor revealed long underwater mountain ranges where new crust forms and spreads outward. Magnetic patterns in the rock on either side matched like mirror images. This showed that the Earth’s surface is made of moving plates, carried by slow currents in the hot mantle beneath. Plate tectonics now explains earthquakes, volcanoes and mountain ranges. Wegener, who died in 1930, did not live to see it.
g: Wegener proposed in 1912 that continents drifted apart, pointing to matching coasts, fossils and rocks.
Geologists rejected it because he had no mechanism to explain how continents could move.
Ocean-floor mapping in the 1950s–60s showed spreading crust, so plate tectonics became accepted after Wegener’s death.
k: Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912 using fossils, rocks and matching coasts.
It was rejected because he lacked a mechanism.
Ocean-floor spreading and magnetic patterns confirmed plate tectonics in the 1960s.

mc.s: What is the passage mainly about?
o: How the idea of moving continents went from rejected to accepted
mc.e: It follows the theory from proposal through rejection to confirmation.

mc.s: What does the story suggest scientists need before accepting a theory?
o: Both evidence and a plausible mechanism
mc.e: Wegener had evidence but no mechanism; acceptance came when the mechanism was found.

mc.s: How does the third paragraph relate to the second?
o: It explains what finally answered the objection in the second
It changes the subject to volcanoes
mc.e: The second paragraph gives the missing mechanism; the third shows how it was found.

v.d: A far-fetched idea seems exaggerated or improbable.

o: the process by which something happens
v.d: A mechanism is how something works or happens.

passages.q: How do Mumbai’s dabbawalas deliver so many lunches so reliably?
p: Every working day in Mumbai, thousands of dabbawalas collect hot home-cooked lunches in metal tiffin boxes from homes, carry them across the city to offices, and later return the empty boxes. The service has run for well over a century and moves around two hundred thousand lunches a day.

The system relies on simple tools rather than technology. Each box carries a short code of coloured symbols and characters showing its collection area, the railway station it travels to, and the destination building and floor. Boxes are sorted at stations, moved in bulk on suburban trains, and re-sorted for final delivery. Many dabbawalas have little formal education, yet they read the codes quickly and precisely.

Researchers and business schools have studied the network for its remarkable reliability. Its strengths include tight timetables built around the trains, a flat organisation where workers share ownership and responsibility, and steady routines that make mistakes stand out. It is a reminder that good operations often come from clear design, not complexity.
g: Dabbawalas deliver about two hundred thousand home-cooked lunches a day across Mumbai, a service over a century old.
It works through a simple coding system and staged sorting via trains, so even workers with little schooling route boxes precisely.
Its reliability comes from timetables, shared ownership and routines, which shows good operations come from clear design.
k: Dabbawalas carry around 200,000 lunches daily and have for over a century.
Coded boxes are sorted in stages and carried on suburban trains.
Reliability comes from timetables, shared ownership and routine: clear design over complexity.

mc.s: What lesson does the author draw from the dabbawalas?
o: Reliable operations can come from simple, clear design
Technology is always needed for reliability
mc.e: The final sentence makes this point.

mc.s: Why might steady routines help reduce mistakes?
o: When everything is routine, an error stands out quickly
Routines make workers faster at running
Routines remove the need for codes
mc.e: The third paragraph says routines make mistakes stand out.

mc.s: What does the code on each box show?
o: The customer’s name and phone number
mc.e: The second paragraph describes these elements.

v.d: Moving goods in bulk means moving many at once.
Precisely means exactly, without errors.

passages.q: How do noise-cancelling headphones remove sound?
p: Sound is a wave of pressure travelling through the air: tiny regions of higher and lower pressure arriving at your ear in quick succession. If two waves meet with their peaks and troughs lined up, they add together and sound louder. If the peaks of one line up with the troughs of the other, they cancel out.

Noise-cancelling headphones use this second effect. Small microphones on the headphones listen to the noise around you. A chip then creates a mirror-image wave, with its peaks where the noise has troughs, and plays it through the speakers alongside your music. The two waves largely cancel, so less noise reaches your ear.

The technique works best on steady, low-pitched sounds such as an aircraft engine or air conditioning, which are predictable. Sudden or high-pitched sounds, like voices or a clattering cup, are harder to cancel in time. That is why headphones combine active cancellation with padded ear cups, which physically block higher sounds.
g: Sound waves add when peaks line up and cancel when peaks meet troughs.
Headphones use cancellation, because they record outside noise and play a mirror-image wave against it.
It works best on steady low sounds, so padding is added to block sudden, high sounds.
k: Sound waves can add together or cancel out.
Headphones detect noise and play an opposite wave to cancel it.
Cancellation works best for steady low sounds; padding blocks high or sudden ones.

mc.s: What does the passage explain?
o: How headphones cancel noise using opposite sound waves, and their limits
mc.e: It explains wave cancellation, its use and its limits.

mc.s: Why are voices harder to cancel than an engine hum?
o: They are less predictable and higher-pitched
mc.e: The third paragraph says sudden or high-pitched sounds are harder to cancel in time.

mc.s: What do the microphones on the headphones do?
o: Record your voice for calls only
mc.e: The second paragraph says they listen to the noise around you.

o: a series of things following one after another
v.d: In quick succession means one after another rapidly.

o: able to be known in advance
v.d: Predictable things behave in a regular way that can be anticipated.

passages.q: Why does spreading study out work better than cramming?
p: In the 1880s the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus spent years memorising lists of nonsense syllables and testing himself. He found that he forgot most new material within days, but that each time he relearned it, it was forgotten more slowly. Spacing out the relearning made the memories last far longer.

Since then, hundreds of studies have confirmed the spacing effect. Information studied in several sessions spread over time is remembered better in the long run than the same amount of study packed into one session, even though cramming can feel more effective at the time. That feeling is misleading: material that feels fluent after cramming often fades quickly.

Why does spacing help? One explanation is that forgetting a little between sessions makes the next session more effortful, and that effort of retrieval strengthens the memory. Practically, this means reviewing new material after a day, then after a few days, then after a week or more, rather than rereading it many times in one evening.
g: Ebbinghaus found that spacing out relearning made memories last much longer.
Many studies confirm spaced study beats cramming, because cramming feels effective but fades fast.
Spacing works because slight forgetting makes retrieval effortful, so review at growing intervals.
k: Ebbinghaus showed relearning spaced over time slows forgetting.
Spaced study beats cramming in the long run, though cramming feels better.

passages.q: How did a trading company come to rule much of India?
p: The English East India Company was founded in 1600 with a royal charter to trade in Asia. It began as a merchant business buying spices, cotton and silk, competing with Dutch and Portuguese traders. For its first century and a half it was mostly a trading enterprise operating from coastal forts.

In the eighteenth century, as the Mughal Empire weakened, the Company became a political and military power. After the Battle of Plassey in 1757 and further wars, it gained the right to collect taxes across large territories, including Bengal. It raised its own armies, largely of Indian soldiers, and by the early nineteenth century controlled much of the subcontinent.

Its rule was increasingly criticised in Britain for corruption and harm, including during famines. After the uprising of 1857, the British government dissolved the Company’s power and took direct control of India in 1858. Historians still study it as an extreme example of what happens when a commercial company holds the powers of a state with little accountability.
g: The East India Company started in 1600 as a trading business operating from coastal forts.
As Mughal power declined, it gained tax rights and armies, so it came to control much of India.
Criticism and the 1857 uprising led Britain to take direct rule, and it is studied as a warning about unaccountable corporate power.
k: The Company began in 1600 as a chartered trading business.
After Plassey (1757) it gained tax rights and armies and controlled much of India.
After 1857 the Crown took direct control; it remains a warning about unaccountable corporate power.

o: It created a power vacuum the Company could exploit
mc.e: The second paragraph links the Company’s rise to the Mughal decline.

passages.q: Why does solid water float on liquid water, and why does it matter?
p: For most substances, the solid form is denser than the liquid, so it sinks. Water is an exception. Ice is about nine per cent less dense than liquid water, which is why ice cubes float and icebergs show only a small part of themselves above the surface.

The reason lies in the shape of water molecules and the way they attract each other through hydrogen bonds. In liquid water, molecules move around and pack fairly closely. As water freezes, the hydrogen bonds lock the molecules into an open, hexagonal pattern with more space between them. The same number of molecules takes up more room, so the ice is lighter for its size.

This quirk is vital for life. When lakes freeze in winter, the ice forms a layer on top that insulates the water beneath, allowing fish and other creatures to survive. If ice sank, lakes could freeze from the bottom up and might stay frozen. The same expansion explains why frozen pipes burst.
g: Ice floats because, unusually, solid water is less dense than liquid water.
Freezing locks molecules into an open pattern through hydrogen bonds, so ice takes up more space.
This matters because floating ice insulates lakes so life survives, and the expansion bursts pipes.
k: Unlike most substances, solid water is less dense than liquid, so ice floats.
Hydrogen bonds lock frozen water into an open pattern with more space.
Floating ice insulates lakes, protecting life; expansion also bursts pipes.

o: Why ice is less dense than water and why that matters
mc.e: It covers the fact, its cause and its consequences.

o: They could freeze from the bottom up and harm life
mc.e: The third paragraph says sinking ice could mean lakes freeze from the bottom up.

mc.s: About how much less dense is ice than liquid water?
mc.e: The first paragraph says about nine per cent.

v.d: A quirk is a strange or unusual characteristic.
To insulate is to reduce the transfer of heat, keeping warmth in.

passages.q: Why does adding more of something eventually give smaller gains?
p: A farmer adds fertiliser to a field and the harvest grows. She adds more and it grows again, but by less. Eventually extra fertiliser adds almost nothing, and too much can even damage the crop. This pattern is called diminishing returns.

It appears whenever one input is increased while others stay fixed. A small team that hires an extra person gets a big boost; a team of fifty that hires one more barely notices, because space, tools and coordination become limits. Studying for an exam shows the same shape: the first few hours help a lot, while the twelfth hour in one day helps little.

Recognising diminishing returns helps with decisions. The question is not whether more of something helps, but whether the next unit helps enough to be worth its cost. Often, the better move is to increase a different input that has become the bottleneck, such as better tools for a large team, or sleep for a tired student.
g: Adding more of an input gives smaller and smaller gains, as with fertiliser, a pattern called diminishing returns.
It happens whenever one input rises while others stay fixed, so extra staff or study hours help less and less.
Decisions should weigh whether the next unit is worth its cost, so often fix the bottleneck instead.
k: Diminishing returns: each extra unit of an input adds less.
It happens when one input rises while others stay fixed, e.g. staff or study hours.
Ask whether the next unit is worth its cost; often fix a different bottleneck.

o: Diminishing returns and how to use the idea in decisions
mc.e: It defines the idea, shows examples and gives decision advice.

mc.e: The final paragraph recommends increasing the input that has become the bottleneck.

passages.q: Why are antibiotics becoming less effective?
p: When Alexander Fleming accepted the Nobel Prize in 1945 for the discovery of penicillin, he warned that bacteria could become resistant to it if the drug was misused. His warning has come true. Infections that were once easily treated are becoming harder to cure.

Resistance is evolution in action. In any large population of bacteria, a few may carry genetic changes that help them survive a drug. When an antibiotic kills the others, the survivors multiply and pass on their resistance. Bacteria can even share resistance genes with one another. Every unnecessary use of antibiotics, in people or in farm animals, gives resistant strains another chance to spread.

The response has several parts: using antibiotics only when they are needed and completing courses as prescribed, preventing infections through hygiene and vaccination, reducing routine use in farming, and developing new drugs. New antibiotics are scientifically difficult and commercially unattractive, since they are used sparingly, so governments are trying new ways to reward their development.
g: Fleming warned in 1945 that misuse would lead to resistance, and infections are now getting harder to treat.
Resistance is evolution: antibiotics kill the weak bacteria, so resistant survivors multiply and spread.
The response combines careful use, prevention, less farm use and new drugs, which need new incentives.
k: Fleming warned of resistance; it is now happening.
Antibiotics select for resistant bacteria, which multiply and share genes; overuse speeds this.
Responses: careful use, prevention, less farm use and incentives for new drugs.

o: Why antibiotic resistance develops and how it can be tackled

passages.q: What did the Wright brothers do differently from other early aviators?
p: At the turn of the twentieth century, many inventors were trying to build a flying machine, some with large budgets and public fame. Wilbur and Orville Wright were bicycle makers from Dayton, Ohio, with modest means. Yet on 17 December 1903, near Kitty Hawk in North Carolina, they made the first controlled, sustained, powered flights.

Their advantage was method. When their early gliders did not lift as expected, they suspected that the published data on wing performance was wrong. In 1901 they built a small wind tunnel and tested around two hundred model wing shapes, producing more reliable figures than existed anywhere. They also focused on control, devising a way to twist the wings so a pilot could balance the aircraft, rather than relying on the machine to be naturally stable.

Others tended to build complete machines and see whether they flew. The Wrights broke the problem into parts, tested each cheaply, and trusted their own measurements over accepted wisdom. Their approach looks very much like what product teams today would call rapid, evidence-driven iteration.
g: The Wright brothers, modest bicycle makers, made the first controlled powered flights in 1903 despite better-funded rivals.
Their method won, because they tested wing shapes in their own wind tunnel and solved control directly.
Unlike rivals, they broke the problem into cheap tests and trusted their data, which resembles modern iteration.
k: The Wrights achieved the first controlled powered flight in 1903 despite modest means.
They built a wind tunnel, tested about 200 wing shapes and solved pilot control.
They broke the problem into parts and tested each: early evidence-driven iteration.

passages.q: Why does losing something feel worse than gaining the same thing feels good?
p: Imagine being offered a coin toss: heads you win £100, tails you lose £100. Most people refuse, even though the bet is perfectly fair. Many want the possible win to be around twice the possible loss before they will play. The pain of losing seems to outweigh the pleasure of winning.

The psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky called this loss aversion and made it central to prospect theory, published in 1979. It helps explain many everyday choices. People hold on to falling shares to avoid “locking in” a loss, and they value things they own more than identical things they do not, a pattern known as the endowment effect.

Businesses and governments use the idea. Free trials work partly because cancelling feels like losing something you already have. Messages framed as avoiding a loss can be more persuasive than the same message framed as a gain. The size of the effect varies across studies and situations, but the basic asymmetry is one of the best-known findings in behavioural economics.
g: People refuse fair bets because losses feel worse than equal gains feel good.
Kahneman and Tversky called this loss aversion, which explains holding losing shares and overvaluing what we own.
Businesses use it in free trials and loss framing, and though the size varies, the asymmetry is well established.
k: Many people reject a fair 50/50 bet because losses feel bigger than gains.
Kahneman and Tversky named loss aversion; it explains holding losers and the endowment effect.
Free trials and loss framing exploit it; its size varies but the effect is well known.

o: Loss aversion and how it shapes behaviour
mc.e: It introduces, names and applies loss aversion.

passages.q: What causes the phases of the Moon?
p: The Moon does not produce its own light. It shines because sunlight reflects off its surface. At any moment, half of the Moon is lit by the Sun and half is in darkness, just as half the Earth is in day and half in night.

As the Moon travels around the Earth, roughly once a month, we see different amounts of its sunlit half. When the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun, its lit side faces away from us and we see a new moon, almost invisible. When it is on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun, we see the whole lit face: a full moon. In between come the crescents and the half moons.

A common misunderstanding is that the Earth’s shadow causes the phases. It does not. The Earth’s shadow only falls on the Moon during a lunar eclipse, which happens occasionally at full moon. The phases are simply a matter of viewing angle: how much of the sunny side happens to be turned towards us.
g: The Moon shines by reflecting sunlight, so half of it is always lit.
As it orbits, we see different amounts of the lit half, which gives new, full and in-between phases.
Phases are not caused by Earth’s shadow, which only matters in eclipses, but by viewing angle.
k: The Moon reflects sunlight; half is always lit.
As it orbits, we see more or less of the lit half: new, crescent, half and full.
Phases come from viewing angle, not Earth’s shadow, which only causes eclipses.

passages.q: How can an insurer promise to pay out for disasters it cannot predict?
p: No one can predict whether their own house will burn down this year. But an insurer covering a million houses can predict, quite accurately, roughly how many will. This is the law of large numbers: individual events are uncertain, but averages across many events are stable.

Insurance turns that stability into a product. Each customer pays a premium, a relatively small regular amount. The insurer pools the premiums and uses them to pay the few customers who suffer losses. Everyone swaps a small, certain cost for protection against a large, uncertain one. The insurer adds a margin for costs and profit, and invests the money it holds in the meantime.

The system has weak points. If people who know they are high-risk buy more insurance, average claims rise; this is called adverse selection. Insured people may also take less care, known as moral hazard. And some risks, such as floods hitting a whole region at once, are correlated, which undermines the law of large numbers because many claims arrive together.
g: Insurers can predict total losses because averages across many cases are stable, even if each case is not.
Insurance pools small premiums to pay the few large losses, so customers trade a small certain cost for protection.
It has weak points, such as high-risk buyers, careless behaviour and correlated disasters.
k: The law of large numbers makes total losses predictable across many customers.
Premiums are pooled to pay the few who suffer losses.
Adverse selection, moral hazard and correlated risks weaken the system.

o: How insurance uses pooled risk and where it can fail
mc.e: It covers the principle, the product and its weaknesses.

passages.q: What is coral bleaching, and why does it happen?
p: Coral reefs look like rocks, but they are built by tiny animals called coral polyps. Living inside the polyps’ tissues are microscopic algae. The algae use sunlight to make food, sharing much of it with the coral, and they give corals most of their colour. In return, the coral provides shelter. Each depends on the other.

When the water becomes too warm for too long, this partnership breaks down. Stressed corals expel the algae, and with them their colour, leaving the white skeleton visible through clear tissue. This is bleaching. A bleached coral is not dead, but it is starving, and if the heat lasts it may die.

Rising ocean temperatures have made mass bleaching events more frequent, affecting reefs such as Australia’s Great Barrier Reef several times in recent years. Reefs can recover if conditions improve, but recovery takes years, and repeated events leave less time between them. Because reefs shelter a large share of marine species, their decline affects fisheries and coastal communities too.

k: Corals and algae depend on each other; algae feed corals and give colour.
Too-warm water makes corals expel algae: bleaching, which can lead to death.
Warming makes bleaching more frequent, leaving less recovery time; impacts reach fisheries and communities.

passages.q: Why did Toyota let any worker stop the production line?
p: On a traditional car assembly line, stopping production was a disaster to be avoided. If a worker noticed a defect, the car usually kept moving, and problems were fixed at the end, if they were caught at all.

Toyota took the opposite approach. Workers could pull a cord, called an andon cord, when they found a problem. A light or signal would alert a team leader, who would come to help. If the problem could not be solved quickly, the line stopped. This seemed wasteful, but it meant defects were tackled at their source, while the cause was still fresh, instead of being built into thousands of cars.

The deeper idea, part of what became known as the Toyota Production System, was that problems should be made visible rather than hidden. Every stop was an opportunity to find and fix a root cause. Over time, the line stopped less often, because the problems that caused stops had been solved. Many software teams now borrow the same principle.

Toyota let workers pull a cord to stop the line, so defects were fixed at the source while causes were fresh.
The principle was making problems visible to fix root causes, so stops became rarer over time.
k: Traditional lines avoided stopping and fixed defects at the end.
Toyota’s andon cord let workers stop the line so defects were fixed at their source.
Making problems visible led to root-cause fixes and fewer stops over time.

passages.q: Why did the world adopt standard time zones?
p: For most of history, every town kept its own time, set by the Sun. Noon was when the Sun was highest, so towns to the west ran a few minutes behind towns to the east. This hardly mattered when travel was slow.

Railways changed that. A train moving across a country passed through dozens of local times, making timetables confusing and collisions more likely. British railway companies began adopting a single standard, London time, from the 1840s, and it became known as railway time. In 1883 North American railways agreed on standard time zones, and in 1884 an international conference in Washington chose Greenwich as the prime meridian, the zero line for longitude.

Today the world is divided into time zones roughly one hour apart, though politics shapes their borders. China, which spans several geographical zones, uses a single official time. India uses one time across the whole country, five and a half hours ahead of Greenwich. The clock on your phone carries the legacy of nineteenth-century train timetables.
g: Towns once kept their own Sun-based time, which was fine when travel was slow.
Railways made local times confusing and dangerous, so standard time and Greenwich as zero were adopted.
Now time zones are roughly hourly but shaped by politics, such as single zones in China and India.
k: Towns once set their own time by the Sun.
Railways drove adoption of standard time: railway time in Britain, zones in 1883, Greenwich in 1884.
Today’s zones are about an hour apart but shaped by politics, e.g. India and China.
